tagline: A 2-million-person metropolis where every road ends at the river — home of the Encontro das Águas, the world's largest floating port, and an Amazon boat culture that already pays a premium for speed on the water.
summary: Manaus sits at the meeting of the Rio Negro and the Solimões, where the two rivers run side by side for kilometres without mixing — the Encontro das Águas, one of the most photographed water spectacles on Earth. Here the river is not a leisure amenity; it is the road network. Regional riverboats, fast 'ajato' launches, vehicle ferries and community lanchas move hundreds of thousands of passengers a year through the city's floating piers, and the federal government is spending R$876 million on a new passenger terminal precisely because demand outgrew the old quays. A foiling-electric layer flies above the river chop and wake conflicts, silent past riverside communities and flooded forest, and shrugs off the extreme seasonal water-level swings that the city's famous floating docks were built to survive.

demand_signals.label: Intermunicipal river passengers
demand_signals.value: 808,462 passengers registered on Amazonas intermunicipal waterway transport in 2023, up 8.63% year on year — with Manaus as the network hub
demand_signals.note: Official state-regulator count; grew even through the severe 2023 drought. Monthly flows run ~56,000+ in peak months
demand_signals.source: ARSEPAM Relatório de Atividades 2023 / Agência Amazonas

demand_signals.label: Federal terminal investment
demand_signals.value: R$875.9M Novo PAC investment in the new Terminal Manaus Moderna — designed for ~3.5 million passengers per year, serving 61 river municipalities and ~4.5 million people, completion 2029
demand_signals.note: One of Brazil's largest waterway passenger infrastructure projects — a design-in window for clean-fleet berthing and charging as the quays are rebuilt
demand_signals.source: Ministério de Portos e Aeroportos / Portos e Navios (May 2026)

demand_signals.label: Speed premium already proven
demand_signals.value: Passengers pay R$380–450 for a fast 'ajato' launch Manaus→Parintins versus a R$150 cap on the conventional riverboat — a 2.5–3x premium for speed that has sustained the Terminal Ajato fast-boat trade for over two decades
demand_signals.note: The Amazon already votes with its wallet for faster water transport; Manaus→Tefé fast-launch fares run ~R$510
demand_signals.source: Porto de Manaus official fare table / Navegam / Veredicto Manauara boat guide

demand_signals.label: Cruise gateway
demand_signals.value: 19 international cruise ships and 25,000+ tourists in the 2023/24 season — the biggest economic injection in the city's cruise history; 16 ships and ~19,000 tourists forecast for 2024/25 (~R$131.8M impact)
demand_signals.note: Every cruise call lands at the floating port and immediately generates Encontro das Águas and jungle-lodge excursion demand

demand_signals.label: The Careiro crossing
demand_signals.value: The CEASA↔Careiro da Várzea ferry is the only link between Manaus and the south-bank BR-319 corridor — vehicle ferries and lanchas run all day from 04:30, with foot passengers paying R$10 and cars R$40–50
demand_signals.note: A captive, daily, all-weather crossing directly across the Encontro das Águas confluence
demand_signals.source: ARSEPAM fare table / G1 Amazonas (ANTAQ-approved 2023 fare adjustment)

use_cases.title: Encontro das Águas, without the diesel
use_cases.body: The city's signature excursion — out from the floating port to where the black Rio Negro and sandy Solimões run side by side unmixed — flown silently on foils above the confluence chop, with zero exhaust over the water that is the attraction itself.

use_cases.title: The Careiro crossing, upgraded
use_cases.body: A scheduled foiling shuttle on the CEASA↔Careiro da Várzea crossing — the captive daily link between Manaus and the BR-319 south bank — smooth, fast and clean where today's passengers queue for vehicle ferries and open lanchas.

use_cases.title: Rio Negro lodge and beach gateway
use_cases.body: Marina do Davi at Ponta Negra is the departure point for jungle lodges, river communities and the Tupé beaches on the Rio Negro's west bank. Foiling transfers turn the lodge run into part of the experience — silent past flooded forest and riverside villages.

use_cases.title: Riverfront cross-town hop
use_cases.body: Manaus traffic funnels through a congested road grid while the Rio Negro runs straight past the city centre. A waterfront line from the floating port to Ponta Negra puts the fastest cross-town trip on the water.

journeys.to: Encontro das Águas confluence + Porto da CEASA
journeys.today: A 6–7 hour diesel tour-boat day trip, or a crowded open speedboat from the CEASA pier for the quick version.
journeys.with_navier: A silent foiling circuit flying above the confluence line where the two rivers meet — no exhaust, no wake slap, back at the pier within the hour.

journeys.today: Queue for the vehicle ferry or squeeze onto an open lancha — the only way across to the BR-319 south bank, from 04:30 to 20:00.
journeys.with_navier: A scheduled foiling shuttle across the confluence — smooth over the mixing-line chop, clean past the fish and produce quays.

journeys.today: A cooperative lancha ride up the Rio Negro to the river beaches and communities — slow, loud, and weather-exposed.
journeys.with_navier: A fast, silent foiling hop up the black-water river to the beach — flying above the wakes, near-zero noise beside the reserve's communities.

journeys.today: A 40–60 minute drive across the city's congested road grid to reach the beach and hotel zone.
journeys.with_navier: A ~15-minute river run along the Manaus waterfront — the fastest cross-town trip in the city, on the water.

journeys.today: Regional lanchas and riverboats work the south-bank villages from the crowded Manaus Moderna quays.
journeys.with_navier: A clean scheduled feeder timed to the new federal terminal — the modern front door for the south-bank communities.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire urban river mesh — the Encontro das Águas circuit (~9 nm one-way loop legs), CEASA↔Careiro (~6 nm), the floating port↔Ponta Negra waterfront (~7 nm), and the Marina do Davi↔Tupé lodge-and-beach run (~10 nm) — sits deep inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope, with marina and port grid power on the Manaus side. Flat, sheltered river water is ideal foiling surface, and the N35 Shuttle's 1.5 ft shallow draft suits floating piers and beach landings across the Amazon's extreme seasonal water-level swings.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The Amazon's long lanes are Quanta-LR territory: upriver to Novo Airão and the Anavilhanas archipelago, and the marquee regional corridors like Manaus→Parintins (~230 nm) where passengers already pay 2.5–3x fares for speed. With 700 nm hybrid range and no charging-infrastructure dependency, Quanta-LR runs the river network as it exists today — no grid required at the far end.

competitive_landscape: The water is already the region's transport backbone: conventional regional riverboats (recreios) and fast 'ajato' launches from the Manaus Moderna quays, vehicle ferries and lanchas on the CEASA↔Careiro crossing, cooperative lanchas from Marina do Davi to Rio Negro communities and lodges, and a large tour-boat fleet working the Encontro das Águas. Demand is proven and regulated — 808,000+ intermunicipal passengers registered in 2023 and an entire fast-boat industry built on speed premiums — but the experience is diesel, loud, and wake-heavy in front of riverside communities. There is no foiling operator on the Amazon system.
seasonality: Manaus runs on the Amazon flood pulse, not a tourist season: the Rio Negro rises and falls over 10 metres a year (record flood 30.02 m in 2021; record drought lows in 2023–24 disrupted navigation region-wide). High water peaks around June; low water runs September–November. The city's famous floating piers exist precisely to ride this range — and shallow-draft foiling vessels keep operating margin in low-water windows that strand deeper conventional hulls. Rain is concentrated December–May; the river itself is sheltered, flat water year-round, with no cyclone exposure.
regulatory_note: The Brazilian Navy (Capitania Fluvial da Amazônia Ocidental) governs vessel class, crew and inland-navigation safety; ANTAQ regulates the mixed crossings and approves fares such as the CEASA↔Careiro table; ARSEPAM, the Amazonas state agency, regulates and registers intermunicipal waterway passenger services; SNPH (the state port and waterway superintendency) plans the organized Port of Manaus, and the Ministry of Ports and Airports with DNIT is delivering the new Terminal Manaus Moderna — an active federal rebuild of the passenger waterfront and a natural design-in window for clean-fleet berthing, charging and low-wake operating standards.
signature_routes: Porto Flutuante ↔ Encontro das Águas ↔ Porto da CEASA (the confluence circuit — the Amazon's most iconic water spectacle)
Porto da CEASA ↔ Careiro da Várzea (the captive south-bank crossing)
Marina do Davi ↔ Praia do Tupé (Rio Negro beach, community and lodge gateway)
Porto Flutuante ↔ Ponta Negra (cross-town waterfront run)

precedents.why_it_matters: Demonstrates electric foiling as the backbone of a water-first transport system at national scale — the proof that a foiling fleet can be the transport layer for a geography where boats, not roads, connect communities.
